subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: Midterm week was in four days when the second milestone slipped. Salma stood at the board in the project room. "Why did the report module miss its date twice?" Because Manu was late finishing. "Why?" He redid it. "Why?" Because the requirement changed. "Why did it change?" There was a silence. Afreen said slowly, "Because we never wrote down what it should do. Each of us remembered it differently." Salma wrote it on the board: unclear requirement, not laziness. Nobody looked defensive now. Between two study sessions they wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what "finished" would mean for each module. Then they sent the page to their guide, and the next milestone was met.

qa.q: What did the team write between the study sessions?
qa.a: They wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what 'finished' would mean for each module.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling when saying the requirement was never written down?
qa.a: Afreen seems reluctant but honest, speaking slowly because it names a shared mistake rather than blaming Manu.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use in future, and why?
qa.a: They could review each requirement together at the start of every milestone, because short check-ins catch differing memories before work is redone.

qa.q: How might Manu see the five-why questions?
qa.a: Manu is asked why he was late and might have felt blamed at first, but the answer shows the cause was the unwritten requirement, so nobody points at Manu.

grounding: Shows root-cause analysis of a missed milestone: repeatedly asking why, finding unclear requirements, and writing a spec with clear completion criteria.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: The second missed milestone hit Arohi's team on a Sunday, in a café near their Bengaluru college. The login and profile module was supposed to be done. Again, it wasn't. Tanvir, who owned it, looked ready to be blamed. Arohi took a napkin. "Let's just ask why. Five times, if we need to." Why isn't it done? Because Tanvir kept rewriting it. Why? Because each time he showed it, someone wanted something different. Why? Because nobody had ever written down what the profile page should include. Why not? Because they'd agreed it on a voice call and everyone remembered it differently. Tanvir let out a long breath. "So I'm not slow. I was chasing a moving target." That evening they wrote a one-page spec for every module, with one line at the top: "Done means it works, it's tested, and all four of us have seen it."

qa.q: Where did the team meet on Sunday?
qa.a: In a café near their Bengaluru college.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel after the whys?
qa.a: Tanvir felt relieved, letting out a long breath on seeing the delay was not laziness but a moving target.

qa.q: What else could the team do when a new idea comes up mid-module?
qa.a: They could add it to the spec only after everyone agrees and adjust the date, so the target doesn't move quietly.

qa.q: How might Arohi see the root cause?
qa.a: Arohi sees it as a team gap in writing things down, not one person's fault, which is why the fix is a spec for every module.

grounding: Shows a team asking why repeatedly after a milestone slips twice, finding unclear requirements rather than laziness, and writing a spec and definition of done.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage:
"That's the second time the dashboard milestone slipped, Nikita."
"I know, Lavanya. I'm sorry."
"I'm not asking for sorry. I'm asking why. Why isn't it done?"
"Because I had to redo the charts."
"Why?"
"Because on Tuesday Rohan said he wanted weekly data, and on Thursday you said monthly."
"...Did I?"
"You did. Why did we say different things?"
"Because we never wrote down what the dashboard is for."
"Why not?"
"Because we thought it was obvious."
"So it's not that you're slow."
"No. It's that nobody knew what finished looked like."
"Okay. Tonight we write one page. Who uses the dashboard, what it shows, weekly or monthly. And a definition of done: it works, it's tested, and all four of us have signed off."
"Can we add: nobody changes it without telling everyone?"
"Yes. That too."

qa.q: What did Rohan want on Tuesday?
How did Nikita feel at the start of the conversation?
qa.a: Nikita felt guilty and on edge, apologising for the slipped milestone.

qa.q: What else could the team do to stop this in other modules?
qa.a: They could write a one-page spec for each module before starting, saying who uses it and what done means.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see the missed milestone by the end?
qa.a: Lavanya realises that a changing request from Lavanya was part of the cause, seeing unclear requirements rather than slowness.

grounding: Illustrates a team repeatedly asking why after a milestone slips twice, tracing it to unclear requirements and agreeing a one-page spec and definition of done.
